[PAPER_0031, relevance_score=0.349] However, based on the existing research and a pilot study, we expected that a positive or negative prior disclosure, by fostering an early preference toward one of the options, would strengthen the top-down control of information selection from subsequent opinions. This process, mediated by the participants' individual attitudes and memories, is likely to be more idiosyncratic than bottom-up control driven by the fixed features of the decision environment.

[PAPER_0070, relevance_score=0.327] We hypothesized that disclosing the adjustment beforehand would make the subsequent eye movements more idiosyncratic. To test this prediction, we considered the average spatiotemporal similarity between the scanpath recorded in a given trial and those of other participants in trials with the same type of disclosure-positive, negative, or none-as the trial in question ("intra-class-similarity"; see the Appendix).

[PAPER_0093, relevance_score=0.304] Here, we aimed to go a step further and demonstrate that eye movement idiosyncrasies can be used to reverse-infer mental states, thus adding a new angle to the debate on whether mental states can be inferred from eye-data (Borji & Itti, 2014).

We considered a setting where choice relevant information was disclosed early or remained hidden until after participants viewed additional evidence. Our hypothesis was that an early privileged information exposure would cause a greater heterogeneity of eye-movements across participants and make their scanpaths more idiosyncratic.

[PAPER_0105, relevance_score=0.310] While not an effect that we expected beforehand, this is consistent with the "density hypothesis" (Alves et al., 2017). This posits that the processing of negative information is more heterogeneous than that of positive information, as illustrated by the famous quote from Leo Tolstoy's Anna Karenina: "Happy families are all alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way." Our results suggest that this principle could potentially apply to "happy" versus "unhappy" decision-makers.

[PAPER_0054, relevance_score=0.257] Data Preprocessing

For each instance of a participant viewing a word grid, we measured the viewing time, the number of words that were looked at, and the overall spatial gaze allocation, particularly the tendency to look at positive versus negative words. Most importantly, we computed an index measuring the extent to which each scanpath was idiosyncratic versus typical. To this end, we calculated a matrix of pairwise spatiotemporal similarities between all scanpaths, and then used a dimensionality-reduction algorithm to map the scanpaths onto a plane in a way that approximates the similarities between them.

[PAPER_0059, relevance_score=0.239] Manipulation Checks

We wished to verify that the participants understood the task and that its various parameters had the desired effect on decisions. Thus, we estimated a mixed-effects binary logistic regression with random subject intercept and slope effects and the investment decision as the dependent variable (1 = invest). Even in the no disclosure condition, the adjustment was still revealed after viewing the word grid and could affect choice.

[PAPER_0060, relevance_score=0.331] Hence, the independent variable set comprised two binary experimental condition indicators ("adjustment-disclosed" and "adjustment-positive"), the interaction between them, as well as a set of controls including the trial number, the proportion of positive words in the grid, and the return obtained in the previous trial (motivated by the effect of past gains on subsequent risky choices, as reported by, e.g., Juechems et al., 2017).

[PAPER_0066, relevance_score=0.281] In this way, no disclosure constituted the baseline category, the "adjustment-disclosed" coefficient measured the difference between no disclosure and a positive one, and finally, "adjustment-disclosed-negative" measured the difference between a negative and a positive disclosure.2 We also included the trial number, the proportion of positive words in the opinion grid, and the return gained in the previous trial as controls. All variables were rescaled to [0, 1] and the full model estimation results are presented in Table 1.

[PAPER_0067, relevance_score=0.237] The first measure was the time of viewing the grid (until pressing a key to move to the decision screen). On average across participants and trials, this equaled 11.5 s. It decreased as the experiment progressed (βtrial-number = 0.097, p < .001) and when the proportion of positive words was higher (βprop-positive = 0.015, p = .028) but increased with the return in the previous trial (βprevious-return = 0.011, p = .001).

[PAPER_0069, relevance_score=0.307] The next measure, "gaze-positivity," represented the tendency to look at grid areas that featured positive words more often (i.e., it did not matter how many positive words one actually saw, but rather which areas of the screen she looked at; see the Appendix for the exact measure specification). It did not significantly vary with any variable apart from the trial number. The average fraction of positive words in areas that were looked at equaled 0.598, slightly above the overall fraction of positive words contained in the grids (59.5%).

This revealed that the smaller the rarer-probability (i.e., the more idiosyncratic the scanpath), the stronger the previously reported positive interaction between adjustment disclosure and its sign (βadj.-disclosed*adj.-pos.*rarer-prob.

[PAPER_0085, relevance_score=0.272] As per our preregistration, we used the following four predictors: (a) the average similarity between the scanpaths making up the set; (b) their average rarer-probability; (c) their average one-dimensional scanpath representation score (used instead of its two-dimensional variant due to the need to average the scores, see the Appendix); and (d) the average number of words seen. As a benchmark, we also evaluated a classifier based on the only noneye tracking measure-the average viewing time across the group.

[PAPER_0054, relevance_score=0.355] Data Preprocessing

For each instance of a participant viewing a word grid, we measured the viewing time, the number of words that were looked at, and the overall spatial gaze allocation, particularly the tendency to look at positive versus negative words. Most importantly, we computed an index measuring the extent to which each scanpath was idiosyncratic versus typical. To this end, we calculated a matrix of pairwise spatiotemporal similarities between all scanpaths, and then used a dimensionality-reduction algorithm to map the scanpaths onto a plane in a way that approximates the similarities between them.

[PAPER_0066, relevance_score=0.252] In this way, no disclosure constituted the baseline category, the "adjustment-disclosed" coefficient measured the difference between no disclosure and a positive one, and finally, "adjustment-disclosed-negative" measured the difference between a negative and a positive disclosure.2 We also included the trial number, the proportion of positive words in the opinion grid, and the return gained in the previous trial as controls. All variables were rescaled to [0, 1] and the full model estimation results are presented in Table 1.

[PAPER_0074, relevance_score=0.241] As described in detail in the Appendix, it was obtained by, first, using the t-SNE algorithm (van der Maaten & Hinton, 2008) to map all scanpaths onto a plane in a way that captures the similarities between them. Next, the distribution of the obtained scanpath representation points was estimated, and the probability of obtaining a rarer point than any given one calculated (see also M. Król & Król, 2019b).
